claim: RPD frequency is not a constant 80%. In Klein's own table it ranges 42-80% across five studies (80% all decision points incl. trivial; 58% expert and 46% novice FGC on hard points; 51% wildfire; 42% tank cadets; 60% design engineers). Ambur reports 46-96% across studies. A pilot simulator study found about one third (34%).
agent_test: Do not hard-code a recognise-first prior. Log which route (match vs compare) the agent takes per item and the accuracy of each route; test a router vs always-match vs always-compare at equal tokens.

claim: Recognitional use rises with experience and time pressure and falls for novices and for organisational decisions (expert 58% vs novice 46%; functional 56% vs organisational 39%).
agent_test: Gate the fast path on a measured familiarity score (similarity to solved cases); compare gated vs ungated at equal tokens.

claim: Evidence on RPD frequency is retrospective interviews, with coders from the research team, a liberal analytic criterion, and no outcome-quality control. Frequency describes reported process; it does not show the process is better.
agent_test: Judge any recognition-first design by outcome accuracy, not by the route the agent reports.

claim: For experts the first option is often good: handball players' first options were rated better than later ones (N=85, 31 scenes), and strong chess players often pick the first generated move.
agent_test: Compare the answer from the first generated candidate vs best-of-k selection at equal tokens on tasks with a rated-quality scale.

claim: The take-the-first advantage needs expertise: in weaker chess players (N=92, Elo under 2000) the first generated move was not better than later ones (F(3,992)=1.73, p=.159) and was judged best only 37.3% of the time.
agent_test: Where the agent has no familiarity signal, scale up the number of candidates; test fixed-1 vs familiarity-scaled option count at equal tokens.

claim: First-move quality depends on task type: experts' first moves were worse in tactical (calculation-heavy) than strategic (pattern-heavy) positions under time pressure (-1.14 vs 2.32, d=0.62).
agent_test: Tag items as pattern-type or calculation-type; allow the fast path only for pattern-type and force simulation or verification for calculation-type.

claim: Time pressure harms even elite players: grandmaster expected blunders per move nearly doubled in blitz (N=20, t(19)=-5.79, d=1.30). Cutting deliberation has a cost that expertise does not remove.
agent_test: Run the same items at low vs high thinking budget and report the loss curve per item class.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-26 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Human mental simulation is small: about 3 moving parts and about 6 transitions. People fall in love with their simulation and explain away contradicting cues (Klein's own list of weaknesses).
agent_test: Cap rollout depth at a few steps; add a forced step that lists one contradicting cue before accepting a simulation; compare at equal tokens.

claim: Direct controlled tests of the mental-simulation step as a causal booster of decision quality in humans were not found; the literature tests frequency and process, not the causal value of simulation.
agent_test: Treat simulation benefit as an empirical question for our agent: A/B with and without a rollout step at equal tokens.

claim: Slow reflective checking helps humans mainly when salient but irrelevant features mislead: residents' correct diagnoses 43% to 52% (N=34, p=.03), no gain in students (24% vs 25%, N=50). Training in reflection did not transfer (N=44, p above .6).
agent_test: Trigger the check only when a salient-but-possibly-irrelevant cue is present or the item is complex; compare triggered vs always-on vs none.

claim: Telling an LLM to reason by recognition-primed decision making raised care-advice accuracy 63.3% to 67.6% (13,500 assessments), but a data-frame prompt did nearly as well (66.7%) and there is no token-matched control, so the gain may come from added reasoning text.
agent_test: Rerun with a length-matched neutral reasoning prompt at equal tokens.

claim: Model-based rollouts with search beat plain chain-of-thought on multi-step planning: Blocksworld LLaMA-33B 2/4/6-step CoT 17/2/0% vs RAP(20) 100/88/42%; Game of 24 ToT b=5 74% vs CoT 4% (GPT-4). The comparisons are not token-matched.
agent_test: Compare search/rollout vs best-of-N sampling at equal tokens on Blocksworld-type and Game-of-24-type items.

claim: Part of the search gain is just more samples: Game of 24 CoT best-of-100 reaches 49%, and plain 25-sample sampling (42%) beats verifier-in-loop back-prompting (36-38%). Snell et al. add that the size of the search gain depends on difficulty: on easy questions heavier verifier-guided search lowered accuracy while best-of-N did not.
agent_test: Always include a best-of-N arm at the same token count.

claim: Search and rollout methods need a capable base model: ToT on Game of 24 gives 74% with GPT-4 but 19% with GPT-3.5, because self-evaluation quality is the limit.
agent_test: Measure evaluator accuracy of our model on labelled partial states before building on rollouts.

claim: LLM self-checking without an outside signal does not help and can hurt: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8 after self-correction; GPT-4 critic loops in Game of 24 5% to 3% and graph colouring 16% to 2%. A sound external verifier gives large gains. A sound external verifier changes this: Blocksworld GPT-4 plan accuracy was 40% unaided, 55% with an LLM critic and 88% with a sound verifier (n=100).
agent_test: Compare self-critique vs sound checker (code execution, constraint check) vs none at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs are unreliable world simulators: best accuracy about 60% on non-trivial state changes (humans 80% vs GPT-4 49% on a matched subset), and rollouts drift over long procedures. Grounding in retrieved tutorials lifted plan alignment from 50-65% to 85-95%. Probe numbers: next-state identification 77-86%, full-procedure plan alignment 50-65% without retrieval and 85-95% with retrieved tutorials (R-WoM, small probe samples).
agent_test: Measure rollout step accuracy against real outcomes on our tasks; limit depth to where accuracy holds.

claim: Imagining each candidate action's outcome and then scoring it (WebDreamer, WMA) beats a reactive agent modestly (17.6 to 23.6 on VisualWebArena, +33% relative) and is far cheaper than real tree search ($0.4 vs $2.7), but real search is still better in some domains (Shopping 28.1 vs 20.8).
agent_test: Candidate then simulate then pick, vs act-first, vs cheap search, at equal tokens.

claim: Fast default plus slow planner on trouble is efficient: SwiftSage 84.7 vs ReAct 36.4 on ScienceWorld with fewer tokens per action (757 vs 1856-2983). It is the closest LLM analogue to simple match then diagnose, but the fast module is fine-tuned, so it is not a pure prompting result.
agent_test: Router: cheap first pass, escalate on a stuck or exception signal; compare against always-slow at equal total tokens.

claim: Letting the model run actions one at a time in a real simulator gave only a small gain on Blocksworld (63.7% to 66.7%) at 5.7 times the tokens and stayed well below a classical planner (85.3%); other papers show larger rollout gains, so the value of simulate-in-environment is contested.
agent_test: Apply environment simulation only where the environment returns a sound signal; compare against plain sampling at equal tokens.

claim: Best rollout depth is not settled. MENSA found depth 3 best and deeper forecasts hurt (ScienceWorld GPT-4o-mini 70.3 vs SSO 54.5 vs ReAct 22.4). Web tree search kept improving up to depth 5 with a value function (VWA 24.5% to 37.0%). In four-in-a-row, reasoning models searched only 1.78 plies on average and depth did not predict wins (beta=-0.015, p=0.82) while breadth did (beta=0.075, p=0.0025).
agent_test: Run depth 1,2,3,5 at equal tokens on our own task classes and record accuracy per class; default cap 3.

claim: Verbal reflection on failed trials helps only where the failure signal is trustworthy: HumanEval 80% to 91% but MBPP 80% to 77% when the test suite had a 0.16 false-positive rate.
agent_test: Gate reflection on a verified failure signal; test with noisy vs clean signals.

claim: Klein's team expected commanders to retrieve and compare past cases but found they rarely reasoned from a specific case; recognition was of typicality.
agent_test: Test prototype summaries vs retrieved case exemplars in memory at equal tokens.

claim: Intuition is valid only where the environment is regular and feedback allows learning (Kahneman and Klein agreement), so a recognition-first path is unsafe in low-validity domains.
agent_test: Estimate the validity of the fast path per task class from held-out accuracy; disable it where near chance.

claim: No study was found that tests an LLM on Klein-style incident decisions scored against human experts; COA-GPT (StarCraft II) is the nearest military case and had more friendly casualties than the human expert.
agent_test: Build a small incident-command item set with expert-rated options if domain transfer matters.

claim: A cheap first-sample gate exists on reasoning benchmarks. Confidence of the first sample (bottom-10% group confidence, AUROC 0.86) accepts 49-61% of GSM8K items at 91-99% accuracy; agreement between a reasoning answer and an executed-program answer resolves 78.6% of items with two samples; Bayesian confidence stopping cuts calls 58% at -0.4 pp. The gate fails where confidence is uninformative (GPQA) and needs per-task calibration.
agent_test: Calibrate the gate (first-sample confidence, 2-3 sample agreement) per task class on a labeled set; disable where AUROC is near chance.

claim: Deliberation pays only where it changes the answer. In a fixed chess position with zero value of computation (12,384 moves) quality did not depend on thinking time; in a high-value position (12,786 moves) quality rose with time and weaker players gained most. For LLM compute, difficulty-adaptive allocation gave over 4x efficiency over best-of-N.
agent_test: Estimate value of computation per item (does a deeper pass change the answer?) before spending a rollout.

claim: Check quality drives most of the check-and-revise gain. Sound verifier 88% vs LLM critic 55% vs none 40% (Blocksworld GPT-4); web tree-search success 24.5% with no value function, 37.0% with a GPT-4o value (n=20 consistency), 43.5% with ground-truth reward; a critical survey finds no success with prompted-LLM feedback except in suited tasks.
agent_test: Prefer executable or rule-based checks; treat a prompted self-check as low-trust and measure its false-positive rate.

claim: A failure-enumeration (premortem) step in the prompt beat a plain safety instruction at similar token counts on professional-ethics tasks (harmfulness 2.19 vs 2.62; zero-shot 3.22), but a forward-direction control with matched structure was indistinguishable under SFT. Effect on task accuracy is untested.
agent_test: A/B a counter-cue step against a length-matched neutral step on accuracy, not safety.

claim: Human evidence for prospective hindsight is thin. The primary paper's abstract reports that temporal perspective had little influence in experiment 1; the popular '30% more reasons' figure was not found in the abstract, and Klein's HBR page has no controlled test. Premortem benefit on decision quality remains unverified.
agent_test: Do not cite the 30% figure. Test the counter-cue empirically in our own harness.

claim: Strategy-level memory beat raw-trajectory and workflow memory on WebArena (684 tasks, Gemini-2.5-flash: 48.8 vs 42.1 trajectories vs 44.1 workflows vs 40.5 none), but the comparison is confounded by use of failures and judged labels.
agent_test: Run the same experience stored as prototype summary vs raw cases at equal tokens.

claim: Retrieval grounding closes much of the multi-step simulation gap where a reference exists: plan alignment 50-65% without and 85-95% with retrieved tutorials, end-to-end relative gains 5.6-23.4% (R-WoM). Single-step accuracy is already above 75%, so the ceiling is long-horizon coherence, not the first transition.
agent_test: Ground each rollout step in retrieved task-specific facts; cap unreferenced rollouts at 2-3 steps.
